data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a rational choice based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness) rather than inductive probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude itself relies on an inductive assumption that nature is uniform.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' implicitly assumes that past success predicts future success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists actually behave as if they believe the theory is probable, not just preferable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between logical probability (which remains zero or low for universal laws) and corroboration (a report on past performance). The mechanism is 'critical preferability': we choose the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it offers the best chance of being close to the truth (high verisimilitude), even though we cannot assign it a higher probability of being true. This is a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action: 'Act as if the best-tested theory is true,' without believing it is probably true.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
